findings.title: Do not execute an unpinned remote script during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads code at build time and executes it as root inside the image with no version pin, commit SHA, checksum, or signature verification. The build is non-reproducible: the same Dockerfile can produce different images on different days, and a compromised, expired, or hijacked host (or a DNS/TLS interception) injects arbitrary code straight into the shipped image and its supply chain. `-L` additionally follows redirects to arbitrary hosts.

findings.title: Pipe to sh masks curl failure and can build a broken image
findings.whyItBreaks: In a shell pipeline the exit status is that of the last command (`sh`), and `curl` here lacks `-f`/`--fail` and the RUN lacks `set -o pipefail`. On a 404/5xx response or a network/DNS/TLS failure, curl emits an empty or error body (and without `-f` may even exit 0 on HTTP error), `sh` reads nothing/partial input and exits 0, so the RUN layer succeeds and the build proceeds to `COPY app /app`/`CMD` with the install step silently skipped. Failure is indistinguishable from success, producing an image missing whatever the installer was supposed to provide.

findings.title: Do not pipe an unverified remote script into sh at image build time
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` runs whatever bytes the remote host returns today as root inside the image build. Nothing pins the script to a version or verifies a checksum/signature: the content of `install.sh` at fetch time is the artifact, so DNS/TLS/CDN/upstream compromise or a simple upstream edit silently injects arbitrary code into every built image. This is a supply-chain surface flagged by `surface: source` (Dockerfile) with build-wide blast radius, and it is not reproducible across builds.

findings.title: curl|sh pipeline swallows download failure and reports success
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline's exit status is `sh`'s, not `curl`'s, and `-s` (no `-f`) means HTTP 4xx/5xx bodies and transient network failures produce empty or HTML input instead of a non-zero curl exit. `sh` on empty/HTML input typically exits 0, so the RUN layer succeeds with the tool never installed; the image then builds 'successfully' and fails only at container start via `CMD ["/app"]` (Dockerfile:5). Compare line 2, where `apk add` failures fail the build immediately: the new step is the first build path that can fail silently.

findings.title: Remove unpinned curl | sh remote code execution from image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added layer pipes a script fetched from https://example.com/install.sh directly into `sh` as root during `docker build`. Nothing pins a version, verifies a checksum/signature, or constrains what that script does, so the image content is not reproducible and anyone who controls example.com (or the DNS/TLS path to it) can execute arbitrary commands in the build environment and bake them into the shipped `/app` image. Additionally, `curl -sL` omits `--fail`, so a 4xx/5xx response body is still piped to `sh` and the build keeps going instead of erroring, silently producing an image with an uninstalled/unknown install step.

findings.title: Don't swallow ErrMissing in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault calls Load and discards its error with `v, _ := Load(key, m)`. Load returns the sentinel ErrMissing (src/store.go:8) exactly when the key is absent, and returns "" for a present key whose stored value is "". Collapsing both paths to "" means every caller of this exported helper is forced to conflate 'key missing' with 'key present with empty value'; it also silently discards any future error type Load may return. There is no default parameter and no doc comment making the sentinel discard an explicit part of the contract, so the API cannot express the failure signal it just dropped.

findings.title: Don't ship exported LoadOrDefault that swallows ErrMissing
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent (src/store.go:7-12) but ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value. LoadOrDefault does `v, _ := Load(...)` and returns only v, so both cases yield "". This is an exported/public API: any caller is now forced to conflate 'key missing' with 'legitimately empty value' and cannot react to a missing config/key (e.g. fail fast, apply a real default, log). The name additionally promises a 'default' it never receives — the only default is the zero value, so callers get silent empty strings where they expect either their default or an error.

findings.title: Make Run wait for spawned goroutines before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, `Run` performed every `results <- j*2` and only returned once all jobs were delivered, so a caller could safely do `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` or drain exactly `len(jobs)` values afterwards. After the change each job is dispatched to a detached goroutine and `Run` returns immediately, so completion ordering relative to `close(results)` is unspecified: the documented-in-code usage pattern now triggers `panic: send on closed channel` in the spawned goroutines, or the caller's drain loop observes fewer than `len(jobs)` results (silent dropped work) because nothing joins the goroutines.

findings.title: Run returns before results are delivered; add WaitGroup before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR Run blocked on `results <- j*2` for every job, so Run returning meant all results had been handed to the channel. Now each send happens in a detached goroutine with no WaitGroup and no completion signal (there is no sync import or Wait anywhere in the file), so Run returns after merely *starting* len(jobs) goroutines while results are still undelivered. Any caller that treats return-from-Run as completion (the natural reading of the old contract, e.g. `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` or proceeding to aggregate/read all results) will either close the channel and get `panic: send on closed channel` from a still-running goroutine, or observe a truncated result set. The channel is send-only (`chan<- int`), so callers have no in-band way to detect that work is still outstanding.

findings.title: Run returns before workers send; goroutines outlive the call
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version Run performed `results <- j * 2` inline, so when Run returned every job had already been delivered to the caller. After the change, Run returns immediately after the loop, while an unbounded number of goroutines are still blocked on `results <- j * 2` (src/worker.go:8). Consequences an exported contract like this permits: (1) a caller that closes or reuses `results` after Run returns triggers `panic: send on closed channel` from the detached goroutines; (2) any consumer that treats 'Run returned' as 'all results are available' (or that exits/aggregates at that point) silently loses results; (3) if `results` is unbuffered and the consumer stops reading (e.g. it only reads len(jobs) values, or hits ctx cancellation), the orphaned goroutines block forever -> goroutine/memory leak, and one goroutine per job means no concurrency bound for large `jobs` slices. The unused `ctx` parameter is not new, but it is now the only cancellation hook and the detached sends do not observe it, so cancellation cannot stop the leaked goroutines.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping: admins must not delete other tenants' records
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously deletion required session.isAdmin AND matching tenantId. With ||, a session with isAdmin=true short-circuits to true regardless of record.tenantId, so an admin of tenant A can delete records owned by tenant B. This is a cross-tenant authorization bypass on a destructive operation.

findings.title: Restore tenant-scoped admin check in canDeleteRecord (&&, not ||)
findings.whyItBreaks: The delete authorization predicate is widened from conjunction to disjunction. With `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId`, two privilege escalations open on every delete path that uses this gate: (1) a non-admin session whose tenantId matches the record now passes, so any tenant member can delete records owned by other users (RecordRef.ownerId is ignored entirely); (2) an admin from any tenant now passes regardless of tenant, so an admin in tenant A can delete records in tenant B. Previously both an admin role AND matching tenant were required, which is the only combination that keeps RecordRef.ownerId/tenantId meaningful. This is a cross-tenant data-destruction bypass, not a behavior tweak.

findings.title: Restore tenant+admin conjunction in canDeleteRecord (auth bypass)
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate previously required BOTH session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId. With `||`, two new unauthorized paths become true: (1) a non-admin session in the same tenant (isAdmin=false, tenantId matches) -> true, allowing any ordinary tenant member to delete arbitrary records in that tenant; (2) an admin of a different tenant (isAdmin=true, tenantId differs) -> true, allowing cross-tenant deletion (confused-deputy / cross-tenant data loss). The predicate is the exported public authorization contract for deletion, so widening it is a live security regression regardless of the current absence of in-repo callers.

findings.title: parseSettings catch-all turns malformed settings into silent DEFAULTS overwrite
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, malformed JSON or invalid theme/fontSize threw, so updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:19-23) aborted at line 20 and its save() callback was never invoked. Now the new `catch { return { ...DEFAULTS }; }` converts every failure (JSON.parse syntax error, the explicit "bad theme"/"bad fontSize" validation throws, and any other exception) into a normal-looking Settings value. updateFontSize cannot distinguish failure from a legitimate value: it mutates fontSize on the defaults object (line 21) and unconditionally calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) (line 22), overwriting a user's existing theme (and any future fields) with "light"/14. This is silent data loss on a live path and also breaks upgrade/legacy data that no longer matches the new strict types. The catch is also on an exported public function with no logging/propagation, so all callers are forced to conflate failure with real settings.

findings.title: Don't persist DEFAULTS after a failed parse; rethrow parse errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The added catch block maps both JSON.parse failures and the 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' validation throws to a legitimate-looking Settings value ({...DEFAULTS}). updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:19-22) consumes parseSettings without any way to distinguish a recovered failure from a real value: it mutates fontSize and unconditionally calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)). Before this diff, a corrupt or partially-invalid raw string caused parseSettings to throw out of updateFontSize and save was never called, preserving the user's existing settings. Now the same failure path resets theme to 'light' (and any other stored fields) and persists that fallback, so a transient read/parse problem destroys user settings rather than leaving them untouched. The exported function also silently discards its own 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' error signals for all future callers.

findings.title: Do not swallow parseSettings validation errors into DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change parseSettings threw on malformed JSON or a bad theme/fontSize, so updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) aborted before calling save(). The new bare `catch` catches both the JSON.parse error and the two validation throws added on lines 11-12 and returns DEFAULTS, so on a corrupt settings blob updateFontSize now writes `{"theme":"light","fontSize":<new size>}` back to disk — silently discarding the user's existing theme/settings and masking the corruption, with no error reaching the caller. The exported parseSettings also now forces every caller to conflate failure with a legitimate default value.

findings.title: buildReport reports artifacts from "verified" ref, not the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `commit` is resolved from the caller-supplied `branch`, but artifacts are now resolved at the hardcoded ref "verified". The returned BuildReport therefore pairs `builtFrom=<branch commit>` with `artifacts=<artifacts of a different/possibly nonexistent ref>`. For any branch whose tip differs from "verified", the report advertises artifacts that were not built from the reported commit (or an empty/wrong list if "verified" does not exist). The change also silently makes the `branch` parameter irrelevant to artifact selection, so every caller of this exported function gets the wrong artifact set.

findings.title: Don't source artifacts from a different ref than builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change buildReport returned { builtFrom: commit, artifacts: build.artifactsAt(commit) }, so the artifacts were guaranteed to correspond to the reported commit. Head now resolves a second, unrelated literal ref ("verified") and passes it to artifactsAt, while builtFrom still reports the requested branch commit. For any build where "verified" points at a different commit than branch (or does not exist), the returned report pairs a build commit with another commit's artifacts — silently misattributing what was built and adding a new failure/mismatch path for callers that only have the branch ref. The two values in the same report are no longer guaranteed to describe one coherent build.

findings.title: Report artifacts no longer come from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport resolves `commit = build.ref(branch)` and reports it as `builtFrom`, but now resolves a second hardcoded ref `build.ref("verified")` and passes that to `artifactsAt`. The returned BuildReport therefore pairs artifacts from 'verified' with a builtFrom value from an unrelated branch/commit. Any consumer trusting builtFrom to describe the artifacts (display, provenance, signing, release notes) gets a wrong mapping; additionally, if the build backend does not have a 'verified' ref for the target (e.g. a feature branch, tag, or older commit), `build.ref("verified")` can fail/throw and break report generation that previously succeeded. The base implementation correctly used `commit` for both.

findings.title: Re-apply slice so recentEntries and renderFeed honor limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The base body returned `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`; the new body builds the reversed copy and returns it unfiltered for any positive limit, so the exported `recentEntries(all, 20)` contract ("Returns at most `limit` entries", line 1) and the `limit` parameter are now dead. renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) still calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and sizes its result around that promise (`new Array<string>(20)` at line 10), assuming page.length <= 20. With 25 inputs, `page.length` is 25, the loop writes indices 20-24 onto the array, and renderFeed returns 25 entries instead of the capped 20 — the feed is no longer bounded.

findings.title: restore limit cap in recentEntries (returns all entries now)
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment and `limit` parameter promise "at most `limit` entries", but the rewritten body only reverses and returns the full array; the `.slice(0, limit)` that actually enforced the cap was removed. The only caller, `renderFeed`, passes 20 and sizes its output from `page.length` (loop at src/feed.ts:11 extends `out` past its 20 slots), so the feed now renders the entire dataset newest-first instead of the 20 newest entries — an unbounded output regression on a public export.

findings.title: Restore limit cap: recentEntries now returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The `limit <= 0` guard was added but the final `.slice(0, limit)` was dropped, so the function returns the entire reversed array for any limit > 0. The unchanged doc carrier on line 1 promises "at most `limit` entries"; the body now ignores `limit` entirely. The in-repo caller `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:9) passes 20 and then writes `page[i]` into `new Array<string>(20)`; with more than 20 entries the writes at indices 20+ extend the array, so renderFeed returns more than the 20-element page it always returned. Any consumer relying on the documented cap (pagination size, fixed-size rendering, downstream slicing) receives an unbounded list instead.

findings.title: Keep entry-count consistent with entries actually rendered
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now emits rows only for non-stale entries (`live`), but still calls headerLines(opts, entries.length), which counts all entries including stale ones. Any consumer that reads the `# entry-count` header to size the body, validate completeness, or reconcile the manifest sees a count larger than the number of rows, causing off-by-N arithmetic/validation failures. Before this change the header and row count agreed.

findings.title: Count only live entries in manifest entry-count header
findings.whyItBreaks: The change filters stale entries out of the emitted rows (line 20-21) but line 22 still passes `entries.length` to `headerLines`. Whenever any entry has `stale: true`, the generated manifest declares `# entry-count: N` for N total entries while containing fewer than N rows. Before this diff, `entries.length` matched the row count exactly; now the header's promise (number of entries in the manifest) diverges from the body output, so a consumer using entry-count for allocation/validation will be wrong.

findings.title: Fix entry-count header after filtering stale entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters rows down to non-stale entries (`live`) but still calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)`. The unchanged header carrier at line 15 promises `# entry-count: ${count}`, and every other manifest entry is emitted from `rows`. With one stale and one live entry, the output is `# entry-count: 2` followed by a single row, so any consumer that sizes, iterates, validates, or reconciles against the declared count sees a mismatch (and a manifest containing only stale entries declares a positive count with zero rows).

After this change every invocation throws, so the function's core path is unusable and any consumer that calls it (or runs the pipeline it represents) crashes on the first call. There is no conditional path, fallback, or feature flag: the failure is total and unconditional.

So an active viewer with attempts < 5 — a legitimately processable request on its own — now gets "rejected" instead of "read-only", a user-facing regression for the entire viewer role. The viewer branch becomes dead code.

findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change an active viewer passed isEligible (base line 14 only checked attempts), and handle() served it via `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` (src/handler.ts:25). The new `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` in the shared gate makes isEligible false for every viewer, so handle() short-circuits at src/handler.ts:24 and returns "rejected". The viewer branch at line 25 is now dead code, and the exported isEligible() contract changes for all external callers: viewers that were eligible are now reported ineligible. The new `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` makes isEligible reject every viewer, so handle() returns "rejected" at line 24 and the viewer branch at line 25 is now dead code. findings.title: Payment gate in canProceed wrongly blocks saveDraft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Gating submit on payment is legitimate, but saving a draft is precisely the action a user takes when payment is still 'missing'. With the new `order.payment === "paid"` conjunct, any draft order with payment: "missing" now returns "blocked" from saveDraft instead of "saved" — a user-facing regression (unpaid drafts can no longer be persisted/kept), even though nothing about saveDraft depends on payment.

findings.title: Payment gate in shared canProceed blocks saveDraft for all drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is read by two distinct actions. submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) legitimately needs paid, but saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) does not. Substituting the normal draft value (state="draft", payment="missing") into the new predicate: order.state !== "ready" is true, order.payment === "paid" is false, so canProceed returns false → `if (!canProceed(order)) return "blocked"` at src/actions.ts:9 → saveDraft returns "blocked" and no draft is saved. Base behavior (git show a246e6b:src/policy.ts) returned true for that input, so this is a regression: drafts can never be persisted because a draft normally has not been paid.

findings.title: Payment gate in shared canProceed wrongly blocks saving unpaid drafts

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the requested channel's head, not "stable"
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot(repo, channel) reports `commit: head` and `channel` for the caller-supplied channel, but the changed line feeds `repo.filesAt(stable)`, where `stable` is `repo.headCommit("stable")` (line 14). Any publish for a non-stable channel (e.g. "main") now returns the stable branch's file list paired with the target channel's commit SHA, so the manifest no longer reflects what was published. It also introduces an unconditional extra `headCommit("stable")` lookup that can fail or return an unrelated/empty ref even when the requested channel is valid.

findings.title: Publish files from the requested channel's commit, not "stable"
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot(repo, channel) resolves `head = repo.headCommit(channel)` and reports it as `commit`, but fetches `files` from `repo.headCommit("stable")`. Any call with a channel other than "stable" (e.g. "main", DEFAULT_CHANNEL) yields a Snapshot whose `commit` points at one tree and whose `files` list belongs to a different tree, so a publish/consumer that reads `commit` (or trusts `files` to describe that commit) ships the wrong content. It also introduces a new dependency on a ref named "stable"; for any Repo implementation that lacks that ref, publishSnapshot now fails where it previously succeeded for the requested channel.

findings.title: Publish reads files from "stable" instead of the requested channel's head

findings.title: Implement `limit` in build() instead of leaving it ignored

The body never references `limit`: it sets `max_count = 10` and iterates `range(max_count)`. Any caller that passes `build(prefix, limit=3)` or `limit=50` gets exactly 10 items regardless, so the promised capping contract is silently unimplemented and the caller receives the wrong data with no error.

findings.title: Honor `limit` in build() instead of ignoring it
findings.whyItBreaks: `def build(prefix, limit=10)` is a public carrier that promises a cap on the number of returned entries, but the body hardcodes `max_count = 10` and `range(max_count)`, never reading `limit`. A caller that writes `build("p", limit=3)` receives 10 elements (and `build("p", limit=0)` receives 10) — a wrong result that differs from the parameter's promised semantics.
