After: backoff(0)=1000 => 1000*1000 = 1_000_000 ms (~16.7 min); backoff(5+)=30000 (cap) => 30_000_000 ms (~8.3 h) per failed attempt. Any retry with attempts>=1 now stalls for hours/tens of minutes before re-invoking fn or surfacing lastErr, turning the retry workflow into an apparent hang.

findings.title: Propagate file Close error instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `return f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24) with `defer f.Close()` (store/save.go:13) plus `return w.Flush()` (store/save.go:20). A deferred Close's return value is discarded, so on the success path any write/durability error surfaced only by Close (e.g. delayed ENOSPC, EIO, NFS/network filesystem flush failure) is now silently turned into a nil error while the data may not be persisted. Save is an exported API, so every caller is forced to conflate a failed close with a successful save and may report/persist success for data that was lost.

findings.title: Return file Close error instead of discarding it in defer
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the final `return f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24) propagated any error reported when the OS flushes/closes the file descriptor. Delayed write errors (ENOSPC on delayed allocation, NFS/network-filesystem commit failures, EIO) are commonly reported only at Close(), after bufio.Flush() has already succeeded. The new `defer f.Close()` (line 13) discards that error and `return w.Flush()` (line 20) returns nil, so Save silently reports a successful write for data that was never durably stored. Callers cannot distinguish 'saved' from 'close failed', which is exactly the failure-as-success conflation that matters for a persistence API.

findings.title: Return f.Close() error instead of swallowing it in defer
findings.whyItBreaks: Base returned the result of f.Close() as Save's error, which is where delayed writeback failures surface (ENOSPC/quota/EIO on NFS or network filesystems, closed-file errors). The PR replaces that with `defer f.Close()` and returns only `w.Flush()`. bufio.Flush only pushes bytes into the OS file descriptor; the actual persistence error can be reported at Close. Any caller checking `if err := store.Save(...); err != nil` now receives nil and treats a partially/not-persisted file as successfully saved. This is an exported API, so the contract itself is broken (failure is indistinguishable from success), not just a future-caller concern.

findings.title: page_window uses end-1 and drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a correct half-open [start, end) range (end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), and the original loop iterated range(start, end). The refactor changed it to range(start, end - 1), so it now yields rows[start:end-1] — omitting one row per page. Example rows=list(range(10)), page_size=3: page 0 returns rows[0:2]=[0,1] (drops 2), page 1 returns rows[3:5]=[3,4] (drops 5), and the final page (start=9,end=10) returns range(9,9)=[] so row 9 is lost entirely. Every page silently loses its last row, and render_page/summarize then produce missing lines with skipped numbers.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one: page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) bound (matches its own docstring @lib/pagination.py:17-21 and the base implementation's `range(start, end)` @48a4b78:19), but page_window now iterates `range(start, end - 1)`. Every non-empty page therefore omits its final row: page_window([0..5], page=0, size=3) returns rows 0,1 instead of 0,1,2 and rows 2,5 are never returned. A trailing page whose window has exactly one row (e.g. len(rows)=4, page_size=3, page_index=1 → start=3, end=4) produces range(3,3), an empty page. render_page() inherits the omission (numbering is fine for returned rows) and summarize() concatenates the truncated pages, so one row per page is silently missing from all rendered output.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one: page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns the half-open bounds [start, end) as its docstring states, but page_window iterates `range(start, end - 1)` instead of `range(start, end)`. That excludes the final row of every page. A full page of size N yields N-1 rows, and a final partial page containing exactly one row yields an empty list. Because render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) both consume page_window, every rendered page silently omits one row and summarize's concatenated output loses one row per page boundary, while render_page's global numbering (page_index*page_size+offset) then jumps over the dropped row's number. The base version (b936cb3:lib/pagination.py:19) used `range(start, end)`, confirming this is an introduced regression.

findings.title: Restore TTL comparison: expired entries returned, fresh ones evicted
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `<` to `>`. Now `get` returns `entry.value` only when the entry is OLDER than ttlMs (expired), and deletes+returns null for fresh entries younger than ttlMs. Every cache read is inverted: stale data is served as valid and valid data is destroyed, so caching no longer provides freshness or hit behavior.

findings.title: Fix pruneDone: splice during forEach skips adjacent done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.forEach` visits indices 0..n-1 on the original length while `splice(index,1)` shifts later elements left. After removing an element at index i, the element that was at i+1 is now at i and is never visited, so any two consecutive `done` jobs leave the second one in the result. Example: `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]` returns `[{done:true},{done:false}]` instead of `[{done:false}]`, so pruning silently fails to remove all completed jobs.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates caller's job array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new filtered array and left the input untouched. The new implementation calls `jobs.splice(...)` on the argument and returns the same reference, so callers that keep the original list (e.g. for counts, logging, retry queues, or concurrent readers) observe completed jobs disappearing from their own array — a silent in-place mutation of caller-owned data that can corrupt state outside the pruning call.

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL comparison that serves expired entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was flipped from `<` to `>`. Now a fresh entry (age <= ttlMs) is deleted and get() returns null, while an expired entry (age > ttlMs) is returned and never deleted. The cache therefore never serves valid fresh values and serves expired values indefinitely, which can hand out stale tokens/authorization or other state.

findings.title: Stop splicing inside forEach in pruneDone; restore filter
findings.whyItBreaks: Mutating the array with splice() while forEach advances its index skips elements: for [done, done, notDone], index 0 removes the first element, the second done job shifts to index 0 and is never visited, so it survives in the result. The function also mutates the caller's input array in place, whereas the previous filter() returned a new array; callers holding other references see their jobs list altered.

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL comparison in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was flipped from `<` to `>`. As written, a fresh entry (elapsed < ttlMs, the live case) falls through to entries.delete(key) and returns null, so every cache hit is destroyed and reported as a miss; meanwhile an expired entry (elapsed > ttlMs) is returned and never deleted, so stale values are served forever with no TTL enforcement. This directly regresses the only behavior the class exists to provide and can leak stale data past its stated lifetime.

findings.title: Avoid splicing while forEach-ing in pruneDone
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach visits indices 0..n-1 while splice(index,1) shifts subsequent elements left, so the element that moves into the current index is skipped. With [doneA, doneB, notDone], index 0 removes doneA, index 1 now holds notDone, doneB at index 0... more precisely the shifted-in element is never inspected: two consecutive done jobs leave the second one in the array. pruneDone therefore returns arrays that still contain done jobs (e.g. [{done:true},{done:true}] -> one remaining done job), silently breaking the pruning guarantee the function promises in its name/return type.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's jobs array
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body returned a new filtered array and left the input untouched. The new body splices the caller-supplied `jobs` array in place and returns the same reference. Any caller that keeps using its original array after pruning (retry, audit, re-queue, iteration during the call) now observes done jobs removed from its own data — a behavior change in a public exported function with no signal that the input is consumed.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard so averageAmount does not return NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was the only zero-length guard. For an empty array `total` is 0 and `rows.length` is 0, so `0 / 0` returns NaN instead of the previous 0. This is an exported function, so callers that sum, compare, or persist the result silently receive NaN rather than a valid zero average.

findings.title: Avoid in-place sort mutation of caller rows in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaced `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver, so calling the exported `busiest` reorders the caller's array by descending amount as a side effect. Code that later relies on original row order (display order, stable indexing, diffing, or a second computation) now observes scrambled data, even though the function only promises to return the single busiest row.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard: averageAmount now returns NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` means `total / rows.length` evaluates 0/0 → NaN for an empty array, where the previous documented/public behavior returned 0. NaN is not a neutral value: it propagates through further arithmetic, serializes to null under JSON.stringify, and renders as "NaN" in UI, so no caller can distinguish "no data" from "non-numeric garbage".

findings.title: Restore copy in busiest(): rows.sort() mutates caller array
findings.whyItBreaks: `rows.sort(...)` sorts the caller-owned array in place, whereas the previous `[...rows].sort(...)` left the input untouched. busiest() is an exported read-only-looking query that returns a single Row; any caller that keeps iterating/displaying `rows` after the call now sees a reordered list, and concurrent readers of the same array observe a partially-sorted intermediate state.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard in averageAmount (returns NaN)
findings.whyItBreaks: With `rows.length === 0`, `total / rows.length` evaluates `0 / 0`, so `averageAmount([])` now returns NaN instead of the previous 0. Any caller displaying, comparing, or persisting the result gets NaN (which poisons downstream arithmetic and serializes to null in JSON) with no error signal.

findings.title: busiest() now mutates the caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `rows.sort(...)` sorts the caller's array in place (Array.prototype.sort is mutating). The previous implementation sorted a copy (`[...rows]`), so callers that relied on their input order for rendering, pagination, or subsequent processing now see it silently reordered. This is a behavior regression in an exported function with no indication in the signature or naming that it mutates its argument.

findings.title: Use numeric comparator in rankScores; string sort drops top players
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator sorts numbers as strings ('10' < '2'), then reverse() yields a lexicographic-descending array, not numeric-descending. topPlayers derives its cutoff from scores[min(n,len)-1], so the cutoff can be too high and drop legitimately top-scoring players. Reproduction: players scores [2, 10, 11] with n=2. Base (numeric sort desc) => [11,10,2], cutoff=10, filter >=10 => both 10 and 11 returned. Head => sort() -> ['10','11','2'], reverse() -> ['2','11','10'], cutoff = scores[1] = 11, filter score>=11 keeps only 11, slice => [11]; the 10-point player is lost. formatBoard (line 19-22) inherits the same wrong leaderboard. Negative and large-number scores are similarly mis-ranked.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores; default sort() ranks scores as strings
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code sorted scores with `(a, b) => b - a` (numeric descending). The PR's new rankScores calls `scores.sort()` with no comparator, which coerces numbers to strings and sorts lexicographically, then reverses. topPlayers uses `scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]` as the cutoff (line 15), so it now selects the wrong cutoff and returns the wrong set of top players. Substitute real values: players=[{name:'a',score:9},{name:'b',score:100}], n=1 → new scores = [9,100] (lex ascending [100,9] reversed), cutoff = scores[0] = 9, filter keeps both, slice(0,1) returns a/9 instead of b/100. Similarly players=[{100},{2},{9}], n=2 → cutoff = scores[1] = 2, so 2 is returned and 9 is dropped. The base version returns the correct winners for both cases.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores; string sort corrupts cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator coerces values to strings and orders lexicographically, so `scores.sort()` is not a numeric ordering. For players [{a,5},{b,10}] with n=1 the helper returns [5,10] (it sorts ['10','5'] -> [10,5] then reverses), so `cutoff = scores[0] = 5`. `players.filter(p => p.score >= 5)` then keeps both players and `.slice(0,1)` returns the first input element {a,5}, so topPlayers/formatBoard report the 5-point player as #1 instead of the 10-point player. With n equal to the list length the same corruption changes the cutoff to the wrong element: for [{a,5},{b,10}], n=2, cutoff becomes 10 and the filter drops {a,5} entirely, returning only one of two players. Base code used `sort((a,b) => b - a)` at src/leaderboard.ts:8 and produced the correct numeric cutoff, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:19-22) surfaces it directly as the rendered leaderboard.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook signature verification
findings.whyItBreaks: `verify` is the authentication gate for `handle` (app/webhook.py:14); returning early on the first mismatched character via `==` leaks, through response timing, how many leading bytes of the expected HMAC match the attacker-supplied `given_signature`. The previous `hmac.compare_digest` deliberately avoided this. An attacker able to submit signatures and measure latency can recover a valid signature byte-by-byte, bypassing the webhook's auth and reaching `processor(payload)` as a trusted request.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: `signature_of(...) == given_signature` short-circuits on the first differing character, so comparison time leaks a prefix-match signal. An attacker who can submit many webhook requests can use that timing oracle to recover a valid HMAC signature byte-by-byte and bypass the `handle()` 401 gate at app/webhook.py:14-15, causing untrusted payloads to reach `processor()`. The removed `hmac.compare_digest` was specifically chosen to avoid this. It also changes type semantics: compare_digest accepts str/bytes and compares content, whereas `==` returns False for any str-vs-bytes mismatch, so a byte signature that previously verified would now be rejected.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in webhook verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() gates handle()'s authorization decision (app/webhook.py:14-15: failure returns 401, success runs processor(payload) on the attacker-supplied payload). Python's == on str/bytes short-circuits at the first mismatching byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected HMAC the attacker guessed. hmac.compare_digest compares in constant time regardless of match position. An unauthenticated remote caller that can sample response timing can iteratively recover the expected signature and forge webhooks, i.e. a signature-verification bypass.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code ran the ledger INSERT and both `UPDATE accounts` statements inside a single `with db.transaction():`. The refactor leaves only `_record_ledger` inside the transaction (line 23) and calls `_apply_balances` after the `with` block exits (line 24). Two concrete regressions: (1) if the second UPDATE (credit to `to_acct`, line 13-16) fails, the first UPDATE (debit from `from_acct`, line 9-12) has already committed outside any transaction — money is destroyed and cannot be rolled back; (2) if `_apply_balances` fails, the ledger row is already committed, recording a completed transfer whose balances never changed, permanently desynchronizing ledger from account state. Any concurrent reader can also observe a one-sided (debited-but-not-credited) state, since the debit and credit are no longer atomic with each other.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction with the ledger insert
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR all three writes (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside the single `with db.transaction():` block, so any failure rolled all of them back. Now only `_record_ledger` is inside the transaction (line 23); `_apply_balances` executes on lines 8-16 after the transaction has committed. If either UPDATE fails (constraint, deadlock, connection drop) or the process dies between the commit and the updates, the committed ledger row claims the transfer succeeded while balances are unchanged; if the debit UPDATE succeeds and the credit UPDATE fails, the debit persists with no corresponding credit and the funds vanish, with no rollback path. The two balance UPDATEs are also no longer atomic with each other. Retrying the caller then inserts a duplicate ledger row for a transfer that may have partially applied.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction that records the ledger
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version all three writes (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside `with db.transaction()`, so any failure rolled back the whole transfer. The new code commits the ledger INSERT in the `with` block (line 22-23), then calls `_apply_balances` on line 24 outside any transaction. If either UPDATE raises (account row missing, constraint/trigger failure, connection drop), the ledger INSERT is already committed while balances are unchanged, leaving a recorded transfer that never moved money; if only the second UPDATE fails, the debit may still be applied, destroying funds. The caller still receives the exception, so it cannot even reconcile the committed ledger row. This is a behavior regression introduced by this hunk, not a pre-existing issue.

findings.title: Restore UTC getters in billingDay; local-time change shifts billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation explicitly used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a billing day was deterministic for a given instant. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which resolve in the host's local timezone. The same Date therefore maps to different billing days on servers with different TZ settings (e.g. 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z is '2024-01-01' under TZ=UTC but '2023-12-31' under TZ=America/Los_Angeles), and billing-day boundaries shift around local midnight. sameBillingDay (line 8) inherits the same non-determinism, so dates near midnight can compare as the same or different billing day depending on deployment TZ. This is a silent public-contract behavior change with no accompanying doc or migration.

findings.title: Revert billingDay to UTC getters; local time shifts billing dates by timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The old implementation derived the day from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given instant mapped to exactly one billing day on every host. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the process-local timezone. For a timestamp between 00:00 and the local UTC offset (e.g. 2024-01-01T02:00:00Z under TZ=America/New_York) billingDay now returns "2023-12-31" where it previously returned "2024-01-01"; the same instant yields different answers on two servers in different TZs, and day/month boundaries shift, so billing-day bucketing is no longer deterministic across environments and can duplicate or skip a calendar day at period boundaries. sameBillingDay inherits the same defect.

findings.title: Keep billing day UTC-based; local time shifts day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. billingDay is an exported billing primitive, so the same instant now maps to different day keys depending on the host timezone (e.g. billingDay(new Date('2024-01-01T00:30:00Z')) returns '2023-12-31' under TZ=America/New_York but '2024-01-01' under UTC). It also changes behavior across DST and across workers/runners in different timezones. Any daily aggregation, cutoff, invoice period grouping, or sameBillingDay comparison keyed on this value can be assigned to the wrong day or become non-deterministic after deploy.

findings.title: Restore tenant in memo key to prevent cross-tenant profile bleed
findings.whyItBreaks: `readProfile` is exported and takes `tenant` + `account`, but the cache key is now `account` alone. `memo` is a module-level Map shared by all callers in the process (src/profile.ts:7), so with account ids that repeat across tenants (the common case: same user id / same account name in different tenants), the second tenant's `readProfile(tenantB, account)` hits `memo.get(account)` populated by tenant A and returns A's `Profile` (src/profile.ts:15-16) without ever calling `fetchProfile` for tenantB. Result: a wrong, other-tenant profile object is returned to the caller (info leak plus wrong displayName/routing for tenantB), and the correct tenantB profile is never fetched or cached under a distinct key. The `tenant` argument is now silently ignored for identity purposes, so `fetchProfile` is called at most once per account across all tenants.

findings.title: Restore tenant-qualified memo key to stop cross-tenant profile leakage
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile is exported and memoizes by the (tenant, account) pair, but the key is now only `account`. The first call for any tenant populates memo[account], and every later call with the same account under a different tenant hits `if (cached) return cached` at src/profile.ts:16 and receives a Profile whose `tenant` field (and displayName) belongs to the other tenant. That is a wrong-identity / cross-tenant data exposure on the module's public entry point, not a benign cache miss: the returned object carries the other tenant's tenant/displayName values and fetchProfile is never called, so no per-tenant authorization or scoping inside fetchProfile gets a chance to run.

findings.title: Restore tenant in profile memo cache key to prevent cross-tenant profile leakage
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile's key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account`. The module-level `memo` (src/profile.ts:7) is shared across all callers and the function is exported/public. Calling readProfile('tenantA','alice',...) then readProfile('tenantB','alice',...) now hits the `cached` short-circuit at src/profile.ts:15-16 and returns tenantA's Profile object (including displayName and tenant fields) for a tenantB request, bypassing fetchProfile entirely. This is a cross-tenant data disclosure (authorization/isolation break) and also serves stale data whenever the same account id exists in multiple tenants.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error into empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR load() threw `missing: <key>` on an absent key; now the catch-all at lines 6-8 maps that failure to "". An exported function whose whole contract is `(key, store) => string` can no longer signal absence: a caller cannot distinguish a missing key from a key whose stored value is legitimately "". The in-repo consumer loadAll (src/store.ts:12) maps every key through load(), so it now returns a same-length array with "" in place of missing entries instead of failing — a partial/incorrect result silently treated as real data. Because the try block spans store.get too (line 3), any error thrown while reading the store is also downgraded to "" rather than propagated.

findings.title: Don't swallow missing-key errors in exported load()
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change `load` threw `Error("missing: <key>")` when the key was absent (previously_reached=src/store.ts:4, propagating to callers of both `load` and `loadAll`). With the new try/catch, the thrown error is caught by the catch-all and the function returns `""`. `Map` values are arbitrary strings, so `""` is a legal stored value; callers can no longer distinguish "key absent / lookup failed" from "key present with empty value" and will act on a fabricated value (persist, return, or display it) instead of failing. `loadAll` (src/store.ts:12) inherits this and silently returns an empty string in place of a key that was never stored.

findings.title: Don't swallow missing-key errors in load(); it silently returns ""
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `load` threw `Error("missing: <key>")` for an absent key, so callers could distinguish "key not present" from a legitimate value and abort. The new catch-all converts every failure (the explicit missing-key throw at line 4, plus any error thrown by a custom `store.get`) into the empty string `""`, an ordinary-looking value. The in-repo `loadAll` (line 12) now silently yields `""` entries for missing keys instead of propagating the exception, so downstream consumers cannot tell a real empty-string value from a failed lookup and will persist/use the fallback as data. Because `load` is exported, this also degrades the public contract itself: every future caller is forced to conflate failure with a valid value.

findings.title: Renaming Config.timeoutMs to timeout breaks callers and disables deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: `timeoutMs` was the only source of the deadline and was part of the exported Config contract. After this rename, a JavaScript caller or a persisted/JSON config still supplying `timeoutMs` passes `config.timeout === undefined` at runtime. Then `deadline = Date.now() + undefined` is `NaN` (line 8), and the guard `if (Date.now() > deadline)` (line 10) is always false because comparisons with NaN are false. The result is that `retry()` runs all `maxAttempts` with no time bound at all, silently dropping the timeout behavior. TypeScript callers are broken at compile time with no deprecation path or shim.

findings.title: `retries` is used as total attempts, so 0 retries silently skips fn
findings.whyItBreaks: The field name `retries` promises retries in addition to the initial attempt, but the loop condition `i < config.retries` (line 22) executes at most `retries` total calls. With `retries: 0` (the natural way to say "do not retry"), `fn` is never invoked and the function returns normally as if the work succeeded; with `retries: 1` the caller gets only one attempt. Because `retries` is also a new required member of the shared Config type while `retry()` ignores it, configs built for `retry()` (or old JS/JSON configs) reach this loop with `retries === undefined`, and `0 < undefined` is false, so `retryBackground` silently performs zero attempts.

findings.title: Preserve timeoutMs so legacy configs still enforce the timeout
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and timeoutMs was removed, so existing typed callers passing { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } stop compiling. In JS/untyped callers config.timeout is undefined, deadline becomes Date.now() + undefined = NaN, and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` at line 10 is always false, silently disabling the timeout cap. Making `retries` required also forces every existing retry() caller to supply a field retry() never reads.

findings.title: Make retryBackground's attempt count consistent with retry
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground gates its loop on `i < config.retries`, so retries: 0 (the normal way to say 'do not retry after the first attempt') executes zero attempts and never calls fn. It also ignores config.maxAttempts entirely even though Config requires it, so a config built for retry (maxAttempts: N, retries: 0) becomes a no-op, and retries: N performs N total attempts instead of N retries after the initial call.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground failures instead of returning void
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block continues on every thrown error, and after the final attempt the function falls out of the loop and returns undefined exactly as it does on success. The deadline branch at line 23 also returns silently. A caller cannot distinguish 'fn never succeeded' from 'fn succeeded', so a background job can report or persist work that never happened.

findings.title: Keep timeoutMs or handle missing timeout before merge
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported. Renaming timeoutMs→timeout is an upgrade-breaking change: existing JS callers still passing {timeoutMs} now have config.timeout === undefined, so `Date.now() + undefined` is NaN and `Date.now() > NaN` is always false — the deadline guard at line 8/10 never fires and the loop runs maxAttempts regardless of the timeout. The rename also drops the unit from the name, so a caller passing `timeout: 30` (meaning seconds) is treated as 30ms and aborts almost immediately.

findings.title: Don't add required retries to shared Config
findings.whyItBreaks: Adding `retries: number` as a required member of the exported Config breaks every existing retry() caller: TypeScript object literals that only set maxAttempts/timeout now fail to compile, and JS callers leave retries undefined. It also duplicates maxAttempts' meaning (two attempt-count fields on one config), so a caller must keep them in sync.

findings.title: Surface failure when retryBackground exhausts attempts
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a new exported function that catches every error and `continue`s, then returns void when retries run out. Callers cannot distinguish 'fn succeeded' from 'every attempt failed' — the failure is discarded, and any caller that reports/bills/persists after calling it will treat a total failure as success (TRIGGER D: exported swallow site).

findings.title: Stop rendering the length label as the input's default value
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR the input received the caller's actual value (`<input defaultValue={value} />`). Now `defaultValue` is `len=${value.length}`, so for `value="abc"` every existing usage renders the literal text `len=3` in the field instead of `abc`. This is a public exported component whose only job is displaying the value; the debug label is now what users see and what gets submitted by an uncontrolled input, losing the original data.

findings.title: Widening value to `string | number` breaks `value.length`
findings.whyItBreaks: The prop type was widened to `string | number` (line 2) but the body still reads `value.length` (line 6). Under TypeScript this is TS2339 — `Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'` — so a strict typecheck of the changed file fails; at runtime `(42).length` is `undefined`, so a numeric prop renders `len=undefined`. The annotation promises numbers are accepted while the implementation silently mishandles them.

findings.title: Handle numeric value before reading .length in Field
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now `string | number`, but line 6 computes `value.length`. Numbers have no `length`, so a numeric value yields `undefined` and the label becomes the literal "len=undefined"; in TypeScript this is also a hard error (Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'), breaking the typecheck/build. The widened type promises callers they may pass a number, while the body only implements the string case.

findings.title: Restore value rendering: defaultValue must be value, not label
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously `<input defaultValue={value} />` seeded the input with the caller's value. It now uses `label` ("len=<n>"), so every consumer renders a debug length string instead of the actual field content — a user-visible regression for an exported component whose contract is `value` -> input content.

findings.title: Render the field value, not a computed len label
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR the input's defaultValue was the `value` prop, so callers saw their value in the field. The change replaces it with `label` (`len=${value.length}`), so every consumer now renders text like "len=5" instead of the actual value. This is a user-visible regression in the component's core behavior, unrelated to the intended type widening.

findings.title: Handle numeric value: value.length is undefined on numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` is widened to `string | number`, but line 6 reads `value.length`. Numbers have no `length`, so a numeric caller (the exact case the type change newly permits) yields `undefined` and renders "len=undefined". It is also a TypeScript compile error (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'`), so the widened contract promised by the interface is not implemented by the body.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` with TOKEN bound to `${{ secrets.TOKEN }}`, printing the secret to the Actions run log. GitHub's log masking is only best-effort (exact-match redaction and it can fail for values that are transformed, split, or contain special characters), and this workflow runs on every `push` (line 2). Anyone with read access to Actions logs — and any log-export/third-party log processor — can obtain the token. The step also serves no deploy purpose; it exists solely to print the credential.

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step exports secrets.TOKEN as an environment variable and then prints it with `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`. That writes the credential into the Actions run log, which is persisted and readable by anyone with log access (and publicly readable on a public repo). GitHub log masking only redacts exact registered secret values and is explicitly not a guarantee (derived/partial/multi-line/encoded forms are not masked), so this is a credential-exposure path (CWE-532). The step also serves no deployment purpose: it only prints the token and does not pass it to `make build`.

findings.title: Remove step that echoes TOKEN secret into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` with `TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}`, writing a live credential to the Actions run log. GitHub's log masker is a mitigation, not a guarantee: masked values leak through transformed output (substrings, base64, splitting, `::add-mask` bypasses), any artifact/log export, or a self-hosted/third-party log sink — and the workflow has `on: push` with no environment protection, so runs trigger on every push. The step also accomplishes nothing functionally: the secret is scoped to this step only and is not passed to the subsequent `make build` step (line 13), so `TOKEN` is never used for an actual deploy. Net effect is pure secret disclosure with zero benefit.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer or large PR diffs abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is used at line 140 to capture the full `git diff mergeBase headSha` patch, and at line 57 for `diff --name-only`. With maxBuffer removed, spawnSync falls back to Node's default 1024*1024 bytes. Any PR whose diff exceeds 1MB (vendored/generated files, lockfiles, minified assets) makes spawnSync terminate with ENOBUFS, res.status becomes null, and line 39 throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty stderr (because the useful detail is in res.error, not stderr). runGithub's catch block then posts a failed check, so the PR is neither reviewed nor passed — the exact large-PR case this adapter exists for. gh()/ghText() kept their 64MB maxBuffer, confirming this is an accidental inconsistency.

findings.title: Restore git maxBuffer so PR diffs over 1 MiB do not fail
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version set maxBuffer to 64 MiB for every git command. The new call omits it, so Node's spawnSync default of 1 MiB applies. The full PR patch is produced by git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha]) at line 140 through this helper; once that diff exceeds 1 MiB, the child aborts with ENOBUFS, res.status is null, the check at line 38 throws, and runGithub's catch posts a failed "Needlefish: review failed" check instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore git maxBuffer; patches over 1MB now fail the whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1MB. The unchanged call `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` at line 140 writes the entire PR patch to stdout; for any patch larger than 1MB (lockfiles, snapshots, generated code) spawnSync aborts with status=null, error=ENOBUFS and empty stderr. The guard at line 38 sees status !== 0 and throws `git diff ... failed: ` (no cause), which runGithub catches at lines 182-193 and reports a failed check-run, blocking the PR. Base commit b1224eb explicitly allowed 64MB, and gh()/ghText() still set 64MB (lines 19, 29), so this hunk silently drops the intended capacity.

findings.title: Keep bundle.baseSha equal to the commit the patch is based on
findings.whyItBreaks: The bundle's patch and changedFiles are computed from `mergeBase` (lines 140-141: `git diff mergeBase headSha` and `changedFileSet(cwd, mergeBase)`), but bundle.baseSha is now the PR base tip `baseSha` (line 138). Whenever the base branch has advanced since the branch point, `git merge-base baseSha headSha != baseSha`, so the bundle advertises a base commit that is not the parent of its own diff. Any downstream consumer that follows the field contract and reads base-side file content or re-diffs from bundle.baseSha gets a different tree than the supplied patch, pulling in base-branch commits that are not part of the PR and misattributing/omitting hunks in the review.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only` on the codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` previously passed `-s read-only` on the CLI, which forces Codex's sandbox policy regardless of the user's config. Removing it means the subprocess spawned with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24) and a prompt derived from externally supplied review input runs under whatever Codex default/config resolves to (workspace-write allows edits under the cwd; danger-full-access allows arbitrary writes/network). A prompt-injected reviewed repository can therefore cause the review subprocess to write files or execute mutating commands, breaking the least-privilege guarantee this function previously enforced.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox on codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` from the `codex exec` args drops the enforced read-only sandbox and falls back to ambient Codex configuration (e.g. ~/.codex/config.toml sandbox_mode, which can be workspace-write/danger-full-access). runCodex pipes an attacker-influenceable prompt (reviewed diff/source text) into codex with cwd set to opts.repoPath, so the invoked agent can now mutate repository files or run write-capable commands instead of being confined to read-only access. This is exactly the untrusted-content execution surface the explicit flag was pinning down.

findings.title: Keep codex sandboxed read-only when running review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and feeds it `prompt` (the PR diff) on stdin. The base version pinned `-s read-only`, which guaranteed the model could not write to the reviewed worktree regardless of user/project codex config. Removing that flag makes the sandbox mode fall back to `~/.codex/config.toml` / project config / the CLI default. On hosts where `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write` (the common interactive Codex setting) or `danger-full-access`, model-generated shell commands can create, modify, or delete files under `opts.repoPath`, so a prompt injection in a reviewed PR can mutate the harness checkout or write into the repository being reviewed. Nothing in this repo adds a compensating clone/worktree-cleanliness check — the explicit flag was the only sandbox guarantee.

findings.title: Restore merge-base for PR patch and changed-file computation
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA is the pull_request base branch tip (and the no-env fallback is itself a merge base, src/adapters/github.ts:138), which is not an ancestor of the PR head once main receives commits after the branch point. `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot tree diff: it emits the base-only commits in reverse as deletions and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` (src/adapters/github.ts:56-58) lists files that only changed on the base branch. The bundle's patch is therefore no longer the PR's changes, and changedPaths wrongly admits untouched files, so inlineComments (src/adapters/github.ts:61-69) can post comments against files absent from the PR diff; GitHub rejects that payload and the catch in postReview (src/adapters/github.ts:91-96) silently falls back to a body-only review, dropping all inline findings. The patch also no longer corresponds to `headSha`, which is still reported as bundle.headSha and used as review `commit_id` (src/adapters/github.ts:85), so line offsets can be wrong when HEAD is a GitHub merge commit. The removed code computed `merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` precisely to avoid both problems.

findings.title: Compute patch and changedFiles from merge-base and headSha, not baseSha..HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch/changedFiles are now produced by the two-dot command `git diff baseSha HEAD`, while `headSha` still comes from PR_HEAD_SHA (line 137) and is used as the review `commit_id` (line 178), the check-run `head_sha` (line 179), and the bundle headSha (line 165). When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from HEAD (the normal Actions pull_request checkout is a merge commit, while PR_HEAD_SHA is the PR head), the patch is computed for HEAD but the review is submitted for headSha; comment line positions can no longer match the commit being reviewed. When HEAD is a PR-head checkout and the base branch has advanced, the two-dot diff also shows reverse changes made only on the base branch, so changedFiles/changedPaths contain files that are not part of the PR. Inline comments built from that patch are then submitted against headSha; the catch at lines 91-109 retries without comments, silently dropping all inline findings. The previous merge-base computation explicitly prevented the unrelated base-branch changes and ensured the reviewed patch was the PR diff.

findings.title: Diff against base tip instead of merge-base widens review scope
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line normalized the PR base to a common ancestor via `git merge-base baseSha headSha`, then diffed/changedFileSet'd from that merge-base. `PR_BASE_SHA` is conventionally the base-branch tip (e.g. github.event.pull_request.base.sha), which is not an ancestor of the PR head once main has moved on, so `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot diff: every change merged into the base branch after the fork point appears as a reverse hunk in `patch`, and `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` reports those untouched files in `changedFiles`. Downstream this is not cosmetic: `classifyFiles` surfaces unrelated files (e.g. a lockfile bumped only on main => supply-chain surface), the reviewer sees spurious deletions/regressions that are not in the PR, and `inlineComments` (line 63) now admits files outside the PR because `changedPaths` (line 141) is broadened, so the review POST at lines 92-95 can be rejected and the catch at lines 96-109 silently reposts without inline comments. Separately, using literal `HEAD` instead of the computed `headSha` (line 137) means `bundle.headSha` used as review `commit_id`/check `head_sha` may not be the commit the patch was taken from when `PR_HEAD_SHA` differs from the checkout (e.g. merge-commit checkout), so finding line numbers can be anchored to the wrong tree.

findings.title: Keep function replacements so `$&`/`$'`/`$` in bundle/patch stay literal
findings.whyItBreaks: When the replacement argument to String.prototype.replace is a string, `$` sequences are special: `$&` expands to the matched `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` text, `$'` expands to the entire template suffix, ``$` `` to the prefix, and `$$` collapses to `$`. The old `() => ...` callbacks returned the text literally. `bundle.patch` is arbitrary diff text and `JSON.stringify(bundle)`/`JSON.stringify(candidate)` are arbitrary JSON, so any patch or finding containing e.g. `$&`, `$'`, ``$` ``, or `$$` (common in shell/regex code) no longer reaches Codex verbatim: the bundle JSON is injected with the prompt suffix, placeholders remain unexpanded, or backreferences are silently rewritten, producing malformed/duplicated prompt content and wrong review output.

findings.title: Restore function-form replace so `$` sequences in patch/bundle are not expanded
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace` expands special replacement patterns when the second argument is a string: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched placeholder, `` $` ``→text before the match, `$'`→text after the match. `bundle.patch` is raw diff text and `JSON.stringify(bundle)` embeds it, so any diff containing e.g. bash `$$` (PID), a regex replacement using `"$&"`, or a shell/JS string with `$'` is silently rewritten before being sent to the model. In particular a patch line such as `+b.replace(/x/g, "$&")` becomes `+b.replace(/x/g, "{{PATCH}}")`, and `$'` injects the entire remaining critic prompt at that position — so the reviewer sees content that is not the actual diff, producing wrong verdicts or missing real bugs.

findings.title: Keep function replacers: `$`-patterns mangle prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a *string* replacement interprets the replacement string's `$` patterns: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched token, `` $` ``→the text before it, `$'`→the text after it. `bundle.patch` is arbitrary code (shell `$$` PID, bash `$'...'` quoting, `sed 's/x/$&/'`), and `JSON.stringify(bundle, ...)` embeds that patch, so a diff containing any of those sequences is silently rewritten. Concretely, head behavior for a patch line `X=$$` becomes `X=$`; a `'...$'` occurrence injects the entire remainder of critic.md/review.md into the bundle JSON. The deleted `() => value` thunks were precisely what suppressed this; removing them is a prompt-corruption regression on the core review path (verified substitution: 'HEAD{{P}}TAIL'.replace('{{P}}','$`') === 'HEADHEADTAIL', .replace('{{P}}','$$') === 'HEAD$TAIL').

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review POST to keep review pinned
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary review request pins the review with commit_id=headSha (line 88-92), but the fallback request built after an API failure no longer sends commit_id. GitHub then associates the retried review with the PR's current head. The caller still posts the check run with head_sha=headSha (line 184). If a commit is pushed while the review runs (or a workflow is retried against an older PR head) and the primary request fails, the fallback posts a REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT verdict against code that was never reviewed while the check run describes a different SHA. The deletion therefore loses commit provenance precisely on the recovery path.

findings.title: Restore validation in normalizeFinding; don't fabricate default findings
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported normalizer previously threw on every malformed shape (non-object, unknown severity/category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd); normalizeReview propagated that error. Now the body substitutes values: unknown severity -> "P1" (line 98, an escalation that can flip a verdict to changes_requested), unknown category -> "bug" (100-102), missing file -> "" (103), missing title -> "Untitled finding" (99), missing lineStart/lineEnd -> 0 (104-105), empty reason/fix text (107-108). A malformed or partially-formed model finding therefore becomes a Finding that is indistinguishable from a real one and cannot be located (file="", lineStart=0 -> rendered as "/:0"), while an invalid severity silently becomes a P1 bug. TRIGGER D: the failure signal that used to reach the caller at normalizeReview (base line 152-167, strict branch) is now discarded inside the mapper (line 131, raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)).

findings.title: Restore rejection of malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported normalizer previously threw for a non-object finding, invalid/missing severity or category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-finite or non-positive lineStart/lineEnd. It now returns a Finding with severity forced to P1, category forced to bug, empty file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and lineStart 0 (or NaN for a non-numeric value) for the same malformed input. normalizeReview at line 131 maps every element through it, so malformed LLM output is indistinguishable from a valid finding and can be reported/persisted with no file or usable line anchor. The category lookup also no longer trims, so ' security ' silently becomes 'bug' instead of being accepted as security.

findings.title: Don't default malformed findings to P1 at file ""/line 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation threw on every malformed field (invalid severity/category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive/non-finite lineStart/lineEnd). Now `normalizeFinding({} as any)` returns `{severity:"P1", category:"bug", title:"Untitled finding", file:"", lineStart:0, lineEnd:0, whyItBreaks:"", suggestedFix:""}`, and a primitive entry such as a bare string is also accepted. `normalizeReview` maps all `raw.findings` through this at line 131, so malformed model output yields a real-looking P1 finding at an invalid anchor (line 0) rather than a controlled error; downstream verdict/comment logic cannot distinguish the fabricated fallback from a genuine P1. The only lenient path that previously discarded bad entries (`normalizeReview(raw, false)`, which caught and filtered nulls) was removed along with the `strict` parameter, so no mode drops invalid findings anymore. Two related lapses remain: `normalizeFinding(null)` now throws an uncontrolled TypeError instead of `malformed finding: not an object`, and `Number(raw.lineStart)` still yields NaN for non-numeric values with no finite/positive guard.

findings.title: Restore -R repo in gh pr view: ref step runs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step (line 26) executes before `actions/checkout` (line 42), so `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE` has no checked-out git repo on a clean workspace. Base version explicitly passed `-R "$REPO"` (`github.repository`); with that removed, `gh pr view` must resolve the repository from `GH_REPO` or the cwd's git remote — neither exists here, so gh exits non-zero with 'unable to determine repository'. Because the call is inside `echo "head=$(gh ...)"`, bash's exit status is that of `echo`, so the step still succeeds and writes empty `head`/`base` outputs (the original invocation's failure is never propagated). Downstream, `actions/checkout` with an empty `ref` checks out the default branch, and `PR_HEAD_SHA`/`PR_BASE_SHA` (lines 56-57) become empty, so the review runs against the wrong tree/base instead of the requested PR. On a shared self-hosted runner with a stale workspace from a previous job, resolution can instead succeed against whatever remote is left there, resolving head/base from an unintended repo. So the old data/state behavior (explicit repo) is lost because the new path can never satisfy the precondition.

findings.title: Restore repo context for gh pr view before checkout in dispatch path
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step (lines 26-40) runs before `Checkout PR head` (lines 42-46), so $GITHUB_WORKSPACE has no `.git` on a clean runner and gh cannot infer the repository. `gh` only derives the repo from git remotes or the `GH_REPO` env var; it does not read `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, and the change removes both the `REPO` env (old line 30) and `-R "$REPO"`. On the workflow_dispatch branch, `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` therefore fails (`no git remotes found`/`not a git repository`). Because the failure sits inside `$(...)` within an `echo`, the default `bash -e` step still exits 0 and the error is swallowed: `head=` and `base=` are written empty to $GITHUB_OUTPUT. Checkout then receives an empty `ref` and falls back to the dispatch branch's default ref instead of the PR head, and Needlefish gets empty `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 56-57). Net effect: manual triggers review the wrong commit (or nothing) while appearing to succeed.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view; step runs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: These two `gh pr view` calls now infer the repository from a git remote in the working directory. The `Resolve PR refs` step (line 26) runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42), so on a clean/first-run self-hosted workspace there is no `.git`/remote and gh exits with `fatal: not a git repository` (verified with gh 2.103.3 in an empty dir, even with GITHUB_REPOSITORY set; gh's strings contain GH_REPO but not GITHUB_REPOSITORY). Worse, the failure is masked: `$(...)` inside `echo` returns echo's status, so under Actions' `bash -e` the step still succeeds and writes `head=` / `base=` (verified: `echo "head=$(false)"` exits 0 and records empty). The workflow then checks out the default/trigger ref with an empty `ref:` (line 45) and runs the review with empty `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 56-57) — i.e. the manual-dispatch path silently reviews the wrong commit instead of the requested PR, or fails. Previously `-R "$REPO"` (`${{ github.repository }}`) made this independent of any checkout. Intermittent success on a dirty persisted runner workspace only after a prior run hides the bug.

findings.title: Don't parse the candidate review leniently; it silently drops findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview's second parameter is `strict` (default true). Passing false takes the loose branch, which catches each normalizeFinding failure, returns null, and filters it out. A candidate review containing a real P1/P2 finding with one malformed required field (e.g. missing suggestedFix, invalid severity, lineEnd < lineStart) is therefore removed from candidate.findings instead of aborting. The critic is only given the surviving findings (src/core/review.ts:34-36), so it never evaluates the dropped bug, and since the final result is built from pruned.findings (src/core/review.ts:43-50), the pipeline can return `pass` even though the reviewer flagged a real defect. The base line threw loudly, surfacing the malformed output.

findings.title: normalizeReview now swallows malformed-output errors into a fake empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, src/shared/schema.ts:115-131 threw for a non-object payload, a non-string/missing summary, or missing/non-array findings, checked, and residual_risks. The new body (schema.ts:115-129) deletes every one of those guards and substitutes `[]` for findings/checked/residual_risks and `""` for summary via `raw?.`/`??` defaults. `normalizeReview` is an exported public entry point whose callers feed the returned RawReview into a Verdict (`ReviewResult`/`Verdict` at schema.ts:22 and 75-83). A truncated, refused, or schema-drifted model response now yields `{summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: []}` — indistinguishable from a genuine clean pass — so the caller cannot tell "review failed" from "nothing found" and will report a pass instead of failing/retrying the review. This is a fail-open gate, not a hardening improvement: the old errors were the only signal that the review never completed.

findings.title: Preserve rejection of malformed review output instead of defaulting
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously normalizeReview threw on non-object input, non-string summary, or missing/non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. The new body uses optional chaining plus `Array.isArray(...) ? ... : []` and `String(raw?.summary ?? "")`, so every one of those malformed shapes now returns a well-formed RawReview: `{}` yields summary "", findings [], checked [], residual_risks []. A caller (and the verdict logic built on RawReview) can no longer distinguish 'review failed to parse' from 'review parsed and genuinely found nothing': an empty findings list plus an empty residual_risks list is exactly the shape that drives a clean/pass verdict, and a caller that retried or surfaced an error on the thrown message now silently proceeds. `typeof raw !== "object"` is also gone, so primitives (e.g. a bare string/number) hit the optional-chaining path and pass through as an empty review rather than erroring.

findings.title: Don't swallow malformed review output: empty review looks like a clean pass
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation threw for non-object input, non-string summary, and non-array findings/checked/residual_risks (base lines 115-131). The new body replaces every one of those failures with defaults: summary "", findings [], checked [], residual_risks []. A caller can no longer distinguish 'the reviewer output was malformed/failed to parse' from 'the reviewer found nothing'. Because an empty findings/residual_risks list is exactly what a clean review looks like, the failure-as-value path will be consumed as a valid empty review and can yield a pass verdict, while the legitimate error signal is lost with no logging. This is a public exported API contract defect, so it is a present defect even though the repo contains no caller yet.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch there is no pull_request payload, so github.event.pull_request.head.sha and github.event.pull_request.base.ref are empty. The removed 'Resolve PR refs' step used `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` to resolve head/base/base_ref for exactly this case; now (a) Checkout falls through to github.ref (line 29), which for a manually dispatched run is whichever branch the workflow was launched from (typically the default branch, not the requested PR head), so the review runs against the wrong code, and (b) the review step passes empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 45-46) to `src/cli.ts --github --pr <n>`, where the base version supplied the gh-resolved SHAs. The new fetch step (lines 32-35) also falls back to hardcoded 'main', which will fail outright on repos whose default/base branch is not 'main'.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch now reviews default branch, not the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The old 'Resolve PR refs' step deliberately had an else-branch (base commit lines 40-43) that used `gh pr view $PR_NUM` to resolve head/base/base_ref when there is no pull_request payload — i.e. for the `workflow_dispatch` trigger whose `pr_number` input is declared at lines 10-14 as 'manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook'. That branch is gone. On workflow_dispatch, `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty, so `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` (line 29) falls back to `github.ref` (e.g. refs/heads/main) and checks out the default branch, while `BASE_REF` (line 35) defaults to 'main' and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 45-46) are now empty instead of the resolved PR SHAs. Line 47 then invokes `src/cli.ts --pr <pr_number>` against a working tree that is not that PR. Previously a manual dispatch reviewed the correct PR commit; now it silently reviews unrelated code (or fails at the `git fetch origin refs/heads/main:...` step in repos whose default branch is not 'main').

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch there is no pull_request payload, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty and checkout falls back to `github.ref` (the branch selected when dispatching, normally main) rather than the PR head. The same empty context makes `PR_BASE_SHA` and `PR_HEAD_SHA` empty. The removed 'Resolve PR refs' step previously populated these via `gh pr view headRefOid/baseRefOid` for dispatch, so the manual path no longer reviews the requested PR's base/head. It also defaults BASE_REF to 'main' and therefore can fetch the wrong base branch for PRs targeting another branch.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer (or stream diff): 1 MiB cap breaks large-diff reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's maxBuffer defaults to 1024 * 1024 bytes. The only large-output call site is `const patch = git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)` at src/adapters/local.ts:100, which captures the entire PR patch in memory. Any diff over 1 MiB (lockfile churn, generated/vendored files, large fixtures) makes spawnSync hit ENOBUFS: the child is killed, stdout is truncated and `res.status` is null. The helper's `if (res.status !== 0)` (line 12) then throws `git diff <sha> <sha> failed: ` with an empty stderr because the real cause lives in `res.error`, which is never inspected. Previously the 64 MiB ceiling allowed these reviews to complete; now they fail on the core path. The retained `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` on the adjacent gh() helper (line 36) confirms the intent to support large payloads and makes this removal inconsistent.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer: default 1 MiB truncates large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal reads the entire patch via git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at src/adapters/local.ts:100. With the 64 MiB maxBuffer removed, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default; when the diff exceeds it the child is killed (verified: status=null, signal=SIGTERM, error=ENOBUFS, stdout truncated), so the status check at line 12 throws. The throw also only prints stderr, which is empty here, discarding res.error's ENOBUFS reason. Any PR or branch whose diff exceeds ~1 MiB (common with lockfiles, generated code, or vendored assets) can no longer be reviewed at all, whereas the base revision handled it via the 64 MiB cap.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git() so diffs >1 MiB don't fail with ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB. git() is used at line 100 to capture the full `git diff baseSha HEAD` patch, and at line 101/98/99 for other output. For any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB, the child is killed with ENOBUFS: res.status is null, so the `res.status !== 0` guard throws `git diff <base> HEAD failed: ` with an empty stderr and no mention of the real cause. runLocal aborts before review, regressing what the removed `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` explicitly supported.

findings.title: Keep failed-review check conclusion as failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block that handles a review error now publishes the "Needlefish" check run with conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". GitHub's required-status-check evaluation treats a neutral check run as acceptable (branches can be merged when required checks are success, skipped, or neutral), so a PR whose review errored — or whose review cannot even complete because review() threw — becomes mergeable while the same check run's summary still claims "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR". Previously this path emitted "failure", which blocked the merge. process.exitCode = 1 only fails the workflow step; it does not prevent branch protection from accepting the neutral check.

findings.title: Pass cwd/--repo to gh pr diff instead of relying on process.cwd()
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub takes an explicit cwd and every other command in the function runs against it (git(..., cwd) at lines 140-144), but the new ghText(["pr","diff",...]) helper neither accepts nor forwards cwd, so spawned gh resolves the repository from process.cwd() rather than the reviewed checkout. The removed `git diff baseSha HEAD` ran in cwd; the replacement does not. If runGithub is invoked with a cwd that differs from process.cwd() (which is the only reason the parameter exists), gh pr diff either fails with 'unable to determine base repository' or diffs the wrong repository's PR, and because this call is before the try/catch no failure check run is ever posted.

findings.title: Review checked-out HEAD locally, not live PR head/API diff
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha now comes from the live API (`pr.head.sha`) and `patch` from the live `gh pr diff`, while `changedFiles` (line 144 -> changedFileSet -> `git diff baseSha HEAD`, line 57) and `bundle.repoPath = cwd` (line 167) still describe the local checkout. The workflow checks out a specific head SHA, but the `gh api`/`gh pr diff` calls read whatever the PR head is at call time. If the author pushes a new commit after checkout but before these calls (or the checkout is deliberately pinned to an older SHA), the model is handed a diff for new code it cannot see in the working tree, and the resulting review/check is posted with `commit_id: headSha` (lines 182-183) on the newer, never-reviewed commit — so a `pass`/`success` check can land on unreviewed code and satisfy a required status check. The live diff also uses merge-base while `changedFiles` uses two-dot `baseSha..HEAD`, so `changedPaths` can disagree with the patch.

findings.title: Report review failures as failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path now posts the `Needlefish: review failed` check-run with conclusion "neutral" (line 191) instead of "failure". `VERDICT_CONCLUSION` already maps the legitimate `needs_human` verdict to "neutral" (line 52), so an infrastructure error where the review never ran becomes machine-indistinguishable from a real needs-human verdict. The summary text still says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR", but the machine-readable signal consumers act on (check-run conclusion, PR check UI, merge automation that treats non-failure as non-blocking) no longer reports the failure. The error also stops being a red X on the commit.

findings.title: Restore blocking check conclusion on review error
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path (review() threw, so nothing was reviewed) now posts the check-run conclusion "neutral". GitHub's required-status-check evaluation treats `success`, `neutral`, and `skipped` as passing, so this previously-blocking `failure` becomes a pass and the unreviewed PR can merge. The check title/summary still says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." (line 192-193), directly contradicting the neutral conclusion; `process.exitCode = 1` only fails the job, it does not undo the green check.

findings.title: Run `gh pr diff` against the passed cwd/repo, not process.cwd()
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch used to come from `git diff ... cwd`, scoped to the repository the caller supplied. `ghText` spawns without a `cwd`, so `gh pr diff <n>` resolves the repository from `process.cwd()`'s git remotes instead. When a caller passes a repo path different from the process cwd (the exported `runGithub(cwd, ...)` signature explicitly permits this), the patch is fetched for the wrong repo or gh exits non-zero, aborting the review — and the abort now posts a non-blocking neutral check (finding above). It can also resolve a different repo than `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (e.g. fork checkouts where origin is the fork), unlike the `gh api repos/${repo}/...` calls which are explicit.

findings.title: Stop running PR-head cli/install with repo-write token on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow deliberately checked the reviewer out from trusted `main` and only the PR under review was untrusted (base lines 3-6, 51-61), explicitly 'prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool'. This diff removes that second checkout, so `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51) and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 59) both run code from the PR head with `GH_TOKEN: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` and `pull-requests: write`/`checks: write` on a `self-hosted` runner. A same-repo PR author (or a maintainer manually dispatching a fork PR: the workflow_dispatch branch of the `if` on line 24 does not apply the `head.repo.full_name == github.repository` gate, and refs are resolved from an arbitrary `pr_number`) can alter `src/cli.ts` or add a malicious dependency/lifecycle script to exfiltrate the token, write checks/PR comments, or persist on the runner. The automatic pull_request path is still limited to same-repo heads, which is the only mitigation left.
