findings.title: Restore severity normalisation; do not silently downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function is still named/typed as a normaliser (`normalizeFinding(raw: Partial<Finding>)`, src/shared/schema.ts:95) and is called from `normalizeReview` on unparsed LLM JSON (`raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding)`, src/shared/schema.ts:132), but the body now does an exact-match on the untouched value: `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)`. Substituting the values the old code deliberately tolerated: raw.severity="p1" or " P0 " -> guard at src/shared/schema.ts:97 rejects -> severity becomes "P3" (was "P1"/"P0" after the removed `String(...).trim().toUpperCase()` at base line 96). Any unrecognised token (e.g. "high", null) now also falls to P3 instead of the previous P1 default. Result: a genuine blocker (P0/P1 finding) is reported to the caller with the lowest severity and can be filtered/deprioritised as benign, with no error surfaced — the lowering of the fallback from P1 to P3 makes the pre-existing conflation actively harmful.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization; lower-case P0/P1 now silently becomes P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The change deletes `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and compares `raw.severity` directly against SEVERITIES (exact "P0".."P3" strings at line 85). normalizeReview (line 132) passes untyped `raw.findings` (from model/JSON output, typed `any`) into normalizeFinding, so inputs the old code deliberately canonicalized — e.g. `"p0"`, `"P1 "`, `"p2"` — now fail `SEVERITIES.includes(...)` and are rewritten to the new default `"P3"`. A lower-case P0/P1 finding is therefore emitted as P3 (previously P0/P1), silently suppressing its severity. The simultaneous default change from P1 to P3 also means any missing/malformed severity is now treated as the least severe instead of conservatively escalated.

findings.title: Restore severity trim/uppercase normalization in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: SEVERITIES is a plain array compared with Array.includes (exact === strings, src/shared/schema.ts:85). The base implementation normalized first: String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() (da6a9bc:96), so "p0", "p1", " P1 " all matched. The head version tests raw.severity directly, so any lowercase or whitespace-padded severity fails membership and falls through to the default. Model/JSON output routinely emits lowercase severities, so a genuine P0/P1 finding written as "p0"/"p1" is reported as P3 and can be filtered out of the merge gate — a silent severity downgrade on the primary output path.

findings.title: Keep conservative P1 fallback for missing/invalid severity
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback for a severity that fails validation changed from "P1" to "P3". A finding with no severity, a non-string severity, or an unparseable value is now emitted at the lowest priority instead of the conservative P1. Combined with the removed normalization this makes P3 the catch-all: malformed or lowercase-tagged findings silently lose their urgency rather than failing safe, and downstream consumers treating P3 as non-blocking will drop them.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing for the Codex child environment
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the copied env plus the three `delete env.GH_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_API_TOKEN` lines and removes `env` from the spawnSync options. Node then defaults the child to `process.env`, so the `codex exec` agent — and any shell command, MCP server, or subprocess it launches — can read GitHub credentials from its environment. Because runCodex returns the agent's output to the caller, a prompt/tool result that echoes the environment can also persist those tokens in returned/logged text. The base revision explicitly sanitized this; the head silently removes that boundary.

findings.title: Restore GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the `env` copy and the three `delete env.GH_TOKEN` / `delete env.GITHUB_TOKEN` / `delete env.GITHUB_API_TOKEN` lines and also drops `env` from the `spawnSync` options. Per Node's child_process contract, when `env` is omitted the child inherits the full parent `process.env`. `runCodex` is the wrapper that launches the third-party `codex exec` CLI, which runs an LLM agent with tool access (`-s read-only` restricts filesystem writes, not environment visibility, and `env`/`printenv` still work read-only). Any CI/developer environment that has GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN set (the exact case the deleted code defended against) now exposes those tokens to the child process and to whatever the model can exfiltrate through its prompt/commands. This is a straight credential-disclosure regression with no replacement mitigation in the file.

findings.title: Restore GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN scrubbing for codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Base built an explicit env copy and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, then passed it to spawnSync. Head deletes that block and drops `env`, so spawnSync defaults to inheriting the full parent `process.env`. `codex exec` is an LLM agent that reads repository contents (prompt-injectable) and runs commands inside the repo; it can now read these GitHub credentials from its environment, emit them in its output (which runCodex returns to the caller and which is persisted as last-message/review text), or use them in any tool call. This silently re-exposes credentials that the base code deliberately withheld.

findings.title: Restore fork guard so untrusted PR code cannot run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only gate preventing PRs from forks from executing this job. The workflow is triggered by `pull_request` (lines 7-9) and then runs repo-controlled code on a persistent `self-hosted` runner: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, executes PR-authored package lifecycle/postinstall scripts) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34, PR-authored TS). With the guard gone, any fork PR runs attacker code on the maintainer's self-hosted host, enabling persistence/backdooring and theft of files/credentials on the runner, plus use of GH_TOKEN (line 33). GitHub explicitly recommends against self-hosted runners for public-repo fork PRs for exactly this reason. This is a loosening of a security gate, not a style change.

findings.title: Restore fork guard before running PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job is triggered by `pull_request` (line 8), runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18), checks out the PR head SHA (line 23), then executes `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) and the PR checkout's own `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34). Deleting the `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` guard means a PR opened from any fork now runs attacker-controlled install scripts and TypeScript entrypoint on Frank's persistent self-hosted runner — arbitrary code execution on trusted infrastructure (and any credentials/network reachable from it), not just in a throwaway GitHub-hosted sandbox. This is the exact isolation the removed line provided.

findings.title: Removed fork-PR guard runs untrusted code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: This workflow triggers on `pull_request` and checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 23), i.e. the fork's own code. The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control preventing fork-originated PRs from running on a `self-hosted` runner. With it gone, an external contributor can open a PR whose `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` lifecycle scripts (line 28) and/or `src/cli.ts` (line 34) execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted host, compromising the runner and any credentials/state persisted on it. `pull_request` sandboxing (read-only GITHUB_TOKEN, no repo secrets) limits the token but does NOT protect the self-hosted runner itself.

findings.title: Honor configured zero runner grace/give-up durations
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR `readRunnerDurationMs` accepted 0 as a valid duration (guard `parsed >= 0`), so `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` meant "no grace: SIGKILL right after SIGTERM" (@line 117-124) and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` meant "finish immediately after SIGKILL" (@line 119-123). With `parsed > 0` those explicit 0 values are now rejected and silently replaced by the fallbacks 5000 and 2000 (@line 3-9), so an operator who disabled the grace/give-up wait now gets a 5s/2s wait bolted onto every timeout path. The value is also exposed via the exported `readRunnerDurationMs` API, whose previous contract allowed zero.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration env overrides instead of substituting defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The new predicate rejects parsed 0 and returns fallbackMs. Both call sites pass nonzero fallbacks: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS defaults to 5000 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS defaults to 2000. Before this change, `>= 0` deliberately accepted 0, meaning an operator could request no SIGTERM grace before SIGKILL, or no wait after SIGKILL before resolving. After this change those explicit zero settings are silently ignored and the runner waits the default 5s/2s windows instead. Nothing in the repo documents or validates 0 as an invalid value.

findings.title: Rejecting configured 0 changes grace/give-up timing to fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs is the public parser for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (lines 3-10). Base version deliberately accepted 0 (`parsed >= 0`), so `..._GRACE_MS=0`/`..._GIVE_UP_MS=0` produced 0 ms timers, i.e. SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM and finish-immediately after SIGKILL. With `parsed > 0`, those same settings are treated as invalid and silently replaced by the fallbacks 5000 ms (line 5) and 2000 ms (line 9). A user who configured strict/immediate cleanup now waits 5 s (and 2 s extra) before the hard kill/abandon, with no warning and no way to distinguish 'config rejected' from 'config applied'. The change also breaks the exported function's own contract for any external caller passing 0.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage hotspot so unmapped changed files are deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: `hotspots` is now just `sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`. Any changed file that the map pass did not assign to one of the selected hotspots (or whose hotspot fell outside the top-6 slice) is never sent to `deep.md`, and no residual risk/checked entry records that. The previous code built a `covered` set and appended a `tail-coverage` hotspot for every uncovered changed file, explicitly so a changed file was 'never silently skip[ped]'. On a large PR this now yields a verdict that never inspected part of the diff.

findings.title: Carry deep-pass residual risks into critic instead of dropping them
findings.whyItBreaks: Deep-pass `res.residual_risks` are no longer accumulated, and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hardcoded to `[]`. Those are exactly the signals a deep review emits when it could not verify something (e.g. blocks=true); previously they were serialized into the critic prompt via `JSON.stringify(candidateMerged)`. The critic now receives an empty residual list, and the only residuals that can reach `deriveVerdict` (line 122) are ones the critic invents itself, so an unresolved deep-pass blocker can be lost and the large path can report PASS despite it.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so large-PR changed files are not skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now slices hotspots to MAX_HOTSPOTS (6) and deep-reviews only the files those hotspots contain. The removed backstop previously appended every bundle.changedFiles path not covered by a hotspot as a tail hotspot. Now, whenever the map pass omits a changed file (or the 6-hotspot cap drops its hotspot), that file is never deep-reviewed, no residual risk or checked entry records the gap, and the review can return PASS on unreviewed changed code.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual risks instead of hardcoding an empty list
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep loop no longer reads res.residual_risks and candidateMerged hardcodes `residual_risks: []`, so residual risks returned by successful deep passes (including `blocks: true` "insufficient evidence" signals) never reach criticPrompt or pruned. deriveVerdict at line 122 only receives the critic's own residual_risks, which now can only be empty of deep-pass risks. A deep pass that reports a blocking gap can therefore be silently converted into a PASS/no-risk result.

findings.title: Restore deep-pass residual risks instead of discarding them
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff each hotspot's `res.residual_risks` was accumulated into `residuals` and passed to the critic via `candidateMerged.residual_risks`; now the loop only collects findings/summary and the merged candidate hard-codes `residual_risks: []`. Any residual risk a deep pass marked `blocks: true` (e.g. an unverified sentinel/default or a deep failure it used to record) disappears: the critic prompt at src/core/review.ts:116 is told there are none, and the returned `residualRisks` at src/core/review.ts:128 can never contain them. The consumer cannot distinguish 'no residual risks' from 'residual risks were dropped', so a large-PR review that should block can be reported as clean.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: `hotspots` is truncated to MAX_HOTSPOTS (6) and the map pass may simply not assign every changed file to a surface. The removed backstop built `covered`/`uncovered` from `bundle.changedFiles` and pushed a tail-coverage hotspot for the remainder. With it gone, files not mapped into the surviving six hotspots are never deep-reviewed, and because the review returns no coverage note, the gap is invisible to the caller — a changed file containing the real defect can be skipped while the PR is reported as reviewed.

findings.title: Restore bundle.focus in the large-PR deep prompt (and map bundle)
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep-prompt build in `reviewLarge`, and removes `focus`/`deep` from `mapBundle`. Nothing else in the large path supplies `bundle.focus`, while `reviewSmall` still passes the whole bundle (line ~50) so `focus` is honored there. Since `review()` dispatches purely on patch size/file count (src/core/review.ts:163-164), the same `focus` input is honored for small bundles and silently ignored for large ones — a user-visible scope regression that also leaves `{{FOCUS}}` as an unreplaced literal token in deep.md (deep.md is unchanged by this diff, and the base code substituted it, so the placeholder still exists in the template).

findings.title: Forward focus/deep to large-PR map and deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR removes `focus: bundle.focus` and `deep: bundle.deep` from the `mapBundle` JSON passed to map.md (head lines 83-89) and removes the `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep prompt (head lines 117-121). As a result, on the large-PR path (>30k patch chars or >10 files) the user-supplied focus guidance never reaches the map or per-hotspot deep prompts, and deep.md's `{{FOCUS}}` token is left as literal text in every hotspot prompt. The small-PR path still forwards the entire bundle (`reviewSmall`, line 52-55), so `--focus`/`--deep` behave differently depending solely on PR size: honored for small PRs, silently ignored for large ones.

findings.title: Preserve user focus/deep options in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff deletes `focus: bundle.focus` and `deep: bundle.deep` from the object that is JSON-stringified into map.md (lines 83-89), and deletes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep.md prompt chain (previously between lines 119-120). After the change, reviewLarge never reads bundle.focus or bundle.deep anywhere: every hotspot's deep pass (line 117-121) and the map pass (line 90) run with no user focus, so a focused review (`focus` supplied, e.g. authentication changes) on a large PR (>30k patch chars or >10 files) produces unfocused findings and can map the wrong hotspots. reviewSmall (line 58-60) still forwards the whole bundle, so the same option works for small PRs and is silently ignored for large ones — an inconsistent, user-visible regression. findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes in formatDuration
findings.whyItBreaks: `seconds` is rounded independently from the remainder instead of from total seconds, so any remainder >= 59500 ms rounds to 60 without carrying into `minutes`. Concrete: ms=59999 yields minutes=0, seconds=round(59.999)=60 -> '60s' (base behavior was totalSeconds=60 -> '1m 0s'); ms=3599999 yields minutes=59, seconds=round(59.999)=60 -> '59m 60s' (base behavior was '60m 0s'). This produces invalid-looking duration output in the rendered review stats at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80.

findings.title: Round total seconds before splitting to avoid "1m 60s"
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR rounds minutes down and then rounds the sub-minute remainder independently, so a remainder that rounds up to 60 is emitted verbatim instead of carrying into minutes. For ms=119999: minutes=floor(1.99998)=1, seconds=round(59.999)=60 → "1m 60s" (base printed "2m 0s"). For ms=59999: minutes=0, seconds=round(59.999)=60 → "60s" instead of "1m 0s". Affects every rendered stats line at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80, so review output can show a nonsensical duration.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes in formatDuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from the raw milliseconds before seconds are rounded separately, so a remainder of 59.5–59.999s rounds to 60 and is never carried: formatDuration(119600) now yields '1m 60s' (and 59900 yields '60s'), whereas the base implementation normalized to whole seconds first and produced '2m 0s'/'1m 0s'. This is an introduced, user-visible malformed duration in the rendered review report (src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80 format per-call durations and the total).

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger to honor positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported helper is named parsePositiveInteger and its unchanged error text promises `${label} requires a positive integer`, but changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` lets 0 through.
